The German name of the operation the Battle of Mortain was fought against.
The German codename of the offensive that the Allies fought as the Battle of the Bulge.
Clipper (Geilenkirchen) ran alongside the Roer-plain offensive on its northern flank.
First Army (Siegfried Line) and Third Army (Lorraine) campaigns ran side by side from September to December 1944.
The pursuit across France followed the closing of the Falaise pocket.

The fighting in the Huertgen Forest overlapped Operation Queen (from 16 November) and was part of the same First Army offensive; the Hürtgen record also covers the Schmidt attack that began on 2 November, so it is not a child of Queen.
Atlantic was launched on 18 July, the day Goodwood opened, on the Canadian front east and south of Caen (Stacey p. 171).
Spring followed Atlantic and Goodwood on the same front (Stacey p. 186, planning from 21 July).
Totalize followed Spring on the same front after the Canadian Army took the corps (Stacey p. 216).
Veritable opened on 8 February; the American Grenade attack by the Ninth Army began on 23 February and the two converged on the Rhine (Stacey pp. 456 and 522).
Varsity, the airborne landing on 24 March 1945, was planned together with Plunder and was timed to follow the first river assaults (Stacey, pp. 531-532; Ellis, vol. II, pp. 286 and 290).
Second Army was reoriented on 16 October 1944 to bring its whole offensive power to bear on the Antwerp situation by a thrust west from s-Hertogenbosch towards Breda (Ellis, vol. II, p. 123).
Infatuate, the capture of Walcheren, was the last land operation of the Battle of the Scheldt and opened the estuary to shipping (Stacey, pp. 379-380; Ellis, vol. II, pp. 123 and 127).
